ex: Hur {firar} man jul i ditt land?
exEn: How do people celebrate Christmas in your country?
The whole family was at the celebration.
note: Action nouns in -ande are ett-words: ett firande, ett leende.

ex: I vår familj är det {tradition} att baka lussekatter.
exEn: In our family, it's a tradition to bake saffron buns.
note: -tion is pronounced 'shoon', and it takes the stress.

exEn: Grandma always cooks traditional Swedish Christmas food.

ex: Jag vill lära mig mer om svensk {kultur}.
exEn: I want to learn more about Swedish culture.
Christmas is the biggest holiday of the year.
note: Usually pronounced 'höktid', with a short ö.

ex: – Är kaffet för varmt? – Nej, det är {lagom}.
exEn: – Is the coffee too hot? – No, it's just right.
note: A Swedish ideal: not too much, not too little. It never changes form: lagom stor, lagom varmt.

exEn: What a cozy café!
note: Also used about evenings and people: en mysig kväll. In everyday speech the g is often silent: 'mysi'.

ex: Vi {myser} i soffan med en film.
exEn: We're getting cozy on the sofa with a movie.
note: The noun is mys: Nu blir det mys! (Time to get cozy!)

ex: I kväll blir det {fredagsmys} med tacos och chips.
exEn: Tonight it's a cozy Friday night in with tacos and chips.
note: A Swedish ritual: snacks and TV on the sofa with the family. Fredag is usually pronounced 'freda'.

ex: Många menar att {jantelagen} lever kvar i Sverige.
exEn: Many people think the Law of Jante lives on in Sweden.
note: An unwritten rule: don't think you're better than anyone else. From a 1933 novel by Aksel Sandemose. Always used in this definite form.

ex: Första maj är en {röd dag}, så jag är ledig.
exEn: May Day is a public holiday, so I'm off work.
note: Public holidays are printed in red in Swedish calendars. Plural: röda dagar.

exEn: What are you doing for Christmas?
note: Holidays are written in lowercase: jul, påsk, midsommar. i jul = this Christmas.

ex: På {julafton} tittar vi på Kalle Anka klockan tre.
exEn: On Christmas Eve we watch Donald Duck at three o'clock.
note: The main day of the Swedish Christmas: the food, the presents and tomten all come on 24 December.

exEn: Merry Christmas, everyone!
note: god sounds like 'go'. Often followed by: och gott nytt år!

exEn: Santa brings presents on Christmas Eve.
note: Also the little gnome of folklore who guards the farm. The Swedish Santa knocks on the door in person!

exEn: What would you like for Christmas?
note: i julklapp = as a Christmas present: Jag fick en bok i julklapp.

exEn: The kids help decorate the Christmas tree.
note: klä granen = decorate the tree. Traditionally it comes down on 13 January (tjugondag Knut).

ex: Vi går på {julbord} med jobbet i december.
exEn: We're going to a Christmas buffet with work in December.
note: Herring, ham, meatballs and much more. Many workplaces book one for their staff.

exEn: The kids drink Christmas soda with the meal.
note: A dark, sweet soft drink sold mainly at Christmas. In December, Swedes drink more julmust than Coca-Cola.

exEn: There's alcohol-free mulled wine too.
note: Served hot in small cups with raisins and almonds, all through December.

exEn: Would you like mulled wine and gingerbread cookies?
note: Literally 'pepper cake'. Swedes joke that eating them makes you kind (snäll).

ex: På {lucia} äter vi lussekatter till frukost.
exEn: On Saint Lucy's Day we eat saffron buns for breakfast.
note: 13 December. Also the girl in white with candles in her hair who leads the procession: Hon är lucia i år.

ex: Min dotter är med i {luciatåget} på förskolan.
exEn: My daughter is in the Lucia procession at preschool.
note: tåg usually means 'train'; here it means 'procession'. Lucia leads, followed by maids, star boys and gingerbread men.

exEn: Shall we bake saffron buns this weekend?
note: An S-shaped saffron bun with raisins, eaten in December. Also called lussebulle.

exEn: We watch the fireworks on New Year's Eve.
note: Often just called nyår: Vad gör du på nyår?

exEn: It's twelve o'clock! Happy New Year!
note: gott and nytt end in -t because år is an ett-word.

ex: I {påsk} ska vi åka skidor i fjällen.
exEn: This Easter we're going skiing in the mountains.
note: Children dress up as påskkärringar (Easter witches) and go door to door for candy.

exEn: The kids are looking for the Easter eggs in the garden.
note: Often a big paper egg filled with candy rather than a chocolate egg.

ex: Vi har ett {påskris} med gula fjädrar i köket.
exEn: We have Easter twigs with yellow feathers in the kitchen.
note: Birch twigs in a vase, decorated with colorful feathers. Here ris means 'twigs', not 'rice'.

exEn: On Walpurgis Night people light big bonfires.
note: 30 April: bonfires and choir songs to welcome spring. Short for valborgsmässoafton.

exEn: I'm taking the bridge day off.
note: A workday squeezed (klämd) between a public holiday and a weekend. Many people take it off.

exEn: Sweden's national day is June 6.
note: A public holiday since 2005. Swedes celebrate it more quietly than many other countries do.

exEn: My little brother graduates from high school in June.
note: On the big day, graduates in white caps run out of school (springer ut) to families holding signs with baby photos.

exEn: Everyone is wearing white student caps in the schoolyard.
note: The white sailor-style cap worn when you graduate from gymnasiet. Often just called mössan.

exEn: We ordered a sandwich cake for the graduation party.
note: A savory 'cake' of bread layered with shrimp, egg and mayonnaise, typical at birthdays and graduations.

ex: Vi firar {midsommar} hos vänner på landet.
exEn: We're celebrating Midsummer with friends in the countryside.
note: Often pronounced 'missommar'. The big party is on midsommarafton, a Friday in late June.

ex: På {midsommarafton} äter vi sill och jordgubbar.
exEn: On Midsummer Eve we eat herring and strawberries.
note: Always a Friday between 19 and 25 June, and in practice a day off for almost everyone.

exEn: Everyone dances around the maypole.
note: Also called majstång. In the classic dance, Små grodorna, everyone hops around like frogs.

exEn: Would you like some more herring?
note: Pickled herring (inlagd sill) with new potatoes is served at every big holiday.

ex: Ska vi ta en {snaps} till sillen?
exEn: Shall we have a schnapps with the herring?
note: A small shot, often of spiced aquavit. Also called nubbe. People sing a snapsvisa before drinking it.

ex: Innan vi skålar sjunger vi en {snapsvisa}.
exEn: Before we drink a toast, we sing a drinking song.
note: The most famous one is Helan går, sung before the first snaps.

exEn: We're having a crayfish party on Saturday.
note: An August party with crayfish, funny paper hats, snaps and songs. sk before i sounds like sj.

exEn: How many crayfish have you eaten?
note: Swedish crayfish are boiled with lots of dill and eaten cold.

exEn: Have you ever tasted fermented herring?
note: Baltic herring fermented in a can, famous for its smell. Open the can outdoors!

ex: Vi har en liten röd {stuga} vid sjön.
exEn: We have a little red cottage by the lake.
note: The classic stuga is painted falu red with white corners.

exEn: We're at the summer cottage all of July.
note: Many Swedish families have one, often in the countryside or the archipelago (skärgården).

ex: Hon köpte en röd {dalahäst} som souvenir.
exEn: She bought a red Dala horse as a souvenir.
note: A hand-painted wooden horse from Dalarna and a symbol of Sweden.
